planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Johnson's Blue is a classic, long-established hardy geranium hybrid with lavender-blue flowers, blooming mainly in a single strong spring flush.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Johnson's Blue, a long-standing classic hardy geranium hybrid dating to the mid-twentieth century, bears large, clear lavender-blue flowers over deeply lobed, attractive foliage, blooming mainly in a strong spring flush with lighter, sporadic rebloom later if deadheaded. Its sprawling, mounding habit weaves attractively through and under other perennials, and it has remained a garden favorite for decades despite the introduction of longer-blooming modern cultivars like Rozanne. In the heat of a zone 9 summer it appreciates afternoon shade and consistent moisture. Shear back hard after the main flush to encourage tidier, fresher growth and possible rebloom.

common_name: Cirrus Mealycup Sage (Silvery-White Foliage and Flower Spikes)

planting.note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost and transplant out after hardening off into well-drained, average soil in full sun; Cirrus bears silvery-white flower spikes and foliage, a striking counterpart to the more common blue and purple mealycup sage selections.

directions: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost and transplant out after hardening off into well-drained, average soil in full sun. Cirrus bears luminous silvery-white flower spikes over soft, gray-green foliage, a bright, cool-toned counterpart to the more common blue and purple mealycup sage selections, useful for a moon garden or as a calming break between more vividly colored companion plants. Extremely heat- and drought-tolerant once established, it flowers continuously from summer through fall with minimal deadheading, drawing bees and butterflies throughout its long bloom season. Deadhead spent spikes to encourage continued bloom, and treat as a perennial in zones 8-10 or a heat-loving annual further north.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes
